title: Raman Effect
short_intro: The Raman effect is the inelastic scattering of a photon by molecules of a substance, resulting in a shift in frequency and wavelength of the scattered light. Discovered by C. V. Raman in 1928, it provides direct evidence for the quantum nature of light and molecular energy levels.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of Raman effect, Rayleigh scattering vs Raman scattering, Stokes and anti-Stokes lines, experimental arrangement, and qualitative wave-number shift.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Quantum mechanical treatment of polarizability, rotational-vibrational Raman spectra, selection rules, calculation of moment of inertia and bond length from rotational Raman lines.

prerequisites: Quantum theory of radiation and photon concept
Molecular energy levels (rotational and vibrational states)

concept_notes.heading: Phenomenology of Raman Scattering
bullets: When monochromatic light of frequency ν<sub>0</sub> is incident on a substance, a major part of the scattered light has the same frequency ν<sub>0</sub> (Rayleigh scattering).
A minute fraction of the scattered light possesses discrete frequencies different from ν<sub>0</sub>, known as Raman frequencies.
Scattered lines with frequencies lower than ν<sub>0</sub> (ν<sub>0</sub> - ν<sub>m</sub>) are called Stokes lines.

concept_notes.heading: Stokes and Anti-Stokes Lines
bullets: Scattered lines with frequencies higher than ν<sub>0</sub> (ν<sub>0</sub> + ν<sub>m</sub>) are called anti-Stokes lines.
Stokes lines originate from molecules in the ground vibrational or rotational state absorbing energy, leaving the molecule in an excited state (ΔE > 0).
Anti-Stokes lines originate from molecules already in an thermally excited state dropping to a lower energy state by giving up energy to the scattered photon (ΔE < 0).

concept_notes.heading: Intensity Distribution and Temperature Dependence
bullets: The intensity of Stokes lines is always greater than the intensity of anti-Stokes lines at room temperature because more molecules populate the lower energy ground state according to the Boltzmann distribution.
As temperature increases, the population of excited states increases, leading to a relative increase in the intensity of anti-Stokes lines.
The Raman shift (Δν) is independent of the incident frequency ν<sub>0</sub> and is a characteristic property of the scattering molecule.

concept_notes.heading: Classical Polarizability Theory
bullets: An incident electric field E = E<sub>0</sub>cos(ω<sub>0</sub>t) induces an electric dipole moment p = αE in a molecule, where α is the polarizability.
If the molecule vibrates with frequency ω<sub>m</sub>, its polarizability varies as α = α<sub>0</sub> + (&partial;α/&partial;q)<sub>0</sub> q<sub>0</sub>cos(ω<sub>m</sub>t).

Substituting α into the dipole moment expression yields terms containing frequencies ω<sub>0</sub>, (ω<sub>0</sub> - ω<sub>m</sub>), and (ω<sub>0</sub> + ω<sub>m</sub>), corresponding to Rayleigh and Raman scattering.

derivations.title: Classical Derivation of Raman Frequencies via Polarizability
derivations.conditions: Harmonic approximation of molecular vibration under an incident electromagnetic wave.
steps: Let the incident electric field be given by E(t) = E_0 \cos(\omega_0 t).
The induced dipole moment is p(t) = \alpha(t) E(t), where \alpha is the molecular polarizability.
Assume the polarizability varies with normal vibrational coordinate q = q_0 \cos(\omega_m t) such that \alpha(t) = \alpha_0 + \left(\frac{\partial \alpha}{\partial q}\right)_0 q_0 \cos(\omega_m t).
Substitute \alpha(t) and E(t) into the dipole moment equation: p(t) = \left[ \alpha_0 + \left(\frac{\partial \alpha}{\partial q}\right)_0 q_0 \cos(\omega_m t) \right] E_0 \cos(\omega_0 t).

Expand the product using trigonometric identities: p(t) = \alpha_0 E_0 \cos(\omega_0 t) + \frac{1}{2} E_0 q_0 \left(\frac{\partial \alpha}{\partial q}\right)_0 [\cos((\omega_0 + \omega_m)t) + \cos((\omega_0 - \omega_m)t)].
derivations.result: The dipole moment oscillates at frequencies \omega_0 (Rayleigh), \omega_0 - \omega_m (Stokes), and \omega_0 + \omega_m (anti-Stokes), proving the existence of Raman shifts.

derivations.title: Rotational Raman Energy Levels and Selection Rules
steps: The rotational energy of a rigid diatomic molecule is given by E_J = \frac{h^2}{8 \pi^2 I} J(J+1) = B hc J(J+1), where B is the rotational constant and J is the rotational quantum number.
The selection rule for pure rotational Raman transitions is \Delta J = 0, \pm 2.
For Raman scattering, the transition J \rightarrow J + 2 gives the energy change \Delta E = E_{J+2} - E_J = B hc [(J+2)(J+3) - J(J+1)] = B hc (4J + 6) for J = 0, 1, 2...
The corresponding wave number shift is \Delta \tilde{\nu} = \pm B (4J + 6).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Raman Spectrum Intensity Distribution
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A central intense Rayleigh line at ν<sub>0</sub>, flanked symmetrically by weaker Stokes lines on the low-frequency side and very weak anti-Stokes lines on the high-frequency side.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Stokes lines are more intense than anti-Stokes lines because the ground state population exceeds the excited state population at room temperature.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in identifying relative intensities and positions of Rayleigh, Stokes, and anti-Stokes lines.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Raman Spectrometer Experimental Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A monochromatic light source (laser or mercury arc), a sample tube (Raman tube) containing the liquid/gas, a collection lens system at right angles, a spectrograph/monochromator, and a detector (photomultiplier or CCD).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Right-angle scattering configuration is used to minimize the entry of direct incident unscattered beam into the detector.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: MCQs regarding optical components and geometric arrangement in UP TGT/PGT exams.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Rotational Raman Spectrum Line Series
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Equidistant spectral lines on either side of the Rayleigh line separated by 6B, 10B, 14B, etc., starting from a gap of 6B from the center.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The spacing between adjacent rotational Raman lines is 4B, allowing direct determination of the rotational constant B and bond length.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical problems calculating moment of inertia or bond length from spectral line separation.

solved_numericals.question: Light of wavelength 435.8 nm is incident on a scattering medium. Calculate the wavelength of the Stokes line for a vibrational frequency shift of 1200 cm<sup>-1</sup>.
solution_steps: Incident wave number \tilde{\nu}_0 = \frac{1}{\lambda_0} = \frac{1}{435.8 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}} = 2.2946 \times 10^6 \text{ m}^{-1} = 22946 \text{ cm}^{-1}.

solved_numericals.question: The spacing between adjacent lines in the rotational Raman spectrum of a diatomic molecule is 1.6 cm<sup>-1</sup>. Find the rotational constant B and the moment of inertia of the molecule. (Given h = 6.626 × 10<sup>-34</sup> J s, c = 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>-1</sup>)
solution_steps: The separation between adjacent rotational Raman lines is given by \Delta \tilde{\nu} = 4B.
Formula for rotational constant: B (in m^-1) = \frac{h}{8 \pi^2 I c}.
Rearranging for moment of inertia I: I = \frac{h}{8 \pi^2 B c}.

solved_numericals.question: In a Raman spectrometer using a laser of wavelength 500 nm, an anti-Stokes line is observed at 480 nm. Calculate the frequency of the molecular vibration responsible for this shift in Hz.
solution_steps: Incident wavelength \lambda_0 = 500 \text{ nm} = 500 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}. Incident frequency \nu_0 = \frac{c}{\lambda_0} = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{500 \times 10^{-9}} = 6.0 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}.

Anti-Stokes wavelength \lambda_{as} = 480 \text{ nm} = 480 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}. Anti-Stokes frequency \nu_{as} = \frac{c}{\lambda_{as}} = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{480 \times 10^{-9}} = 6.25 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}.

assumptions_and_limitations: The classical polarizability theory assumes small oscillations of nuclei compared to intermolecular distances (harmonic approximation), which fails at high vibrational excitation.
Interaction between vibration and rotation (centrifugal distortion) is neglected in simple rigid rotor approximations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Raman scattering is caused by the absorption and subsequent re-emission of a photon, similar to fluorescence.
common_misconceptions.correct: Raman scattering is an instantaneous two-photon scattering process involving virtual energy states, not real electronic transitions.
common_misconceptions.why: Fluorescence involves real absorption to an excited electronic state with a finite lifetime (~10^-8 s), whereas Raman scattering is prompt.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The Raman shift depends upon the wavelength or frequency of the incident light source.
common_misconceptions.correct: The Raman frequency shift (Δν or Δν˛) is strictly a constant for a given molecular transition and is independent of the incident photon frequency.
common_misconceptions.why: The absolute scattered frequencies change with incident frequency, but the difference (ν<sub>0</sub> - ν<sub>s</sub>) remains constant.

quick_revision: Raman effect is inelastic scattering where scattered frequency differs from incident frequency by molecular vibrational/rotational frequencies.
